Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- Iraq's Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Sunday tried to allay Iranian fears over a planned U.S.-Iraq security pact, saying his government would not allow Iraq to become a launching pad for an attack on its neighbor. Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, left, greets Iraq's Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki on Sunday. "Iraq today doesn't present any threat as it used to be in the times of the former regime," al-Maliki told Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad during a Sunday meeting between two leaders, according to a statement from the prime minister's office. "Today's Iraq is a constitutional state based on the rule of law, and it seeks to develop its relations with the regional countries based on cooperation and mutual respect," al-Maliki said. Earlier, Iran's state-run news agency IRNA quoted the Iraqi leader as saying that "Baghdad would not allow its soil to be used as a base to damage the security of the neighboring countries, including Iran." His remarks come as the United States and Iraq are trying to reach a bilateral agreement on how long the U.S. military will remain in Iraq and what role it will play in Iraq's security. But al-Maliki media adviser Ali Hadi said negotiations between Iraq and the United States are in their "very early stages" and were not part of Sunday's talks.  Watch Ahmadinejad and al-Maliki sit down for talks » . "The treaty is purely an Iraqi-American treaty. The Iranians have nothing to do with it," Hadi said. "We will not discuss the progress or the key elements of agreements or disagreements with them because this is an Iraqi issue." The proposed U.S.-Iraqi pact has triggered street protests in Iraq, where many suspect the deal could lead to the establishment of permanent American bases, a long-term presence of U.S. troops and a weakening of Iraqi government control over those troops. Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, whose militia was the target of a U.S.-backed Iraqi clampdown in Basra and Baghdad recently, has called for weekly protests against the agreement. Al-Maliki and Ahmadinejad met Sunday afternoon, with Ahmadinejad calling on Iraq's neighbors and the United Nations to help restore security and stability to Iraq, IRNA reported. And al-Maliki thanked Ahmadinejad for his call for an end to longstanding U.N. sanctions against Iraq that date back to the 1991 Persian Gulf war. Iran has long called for the withdrawal of U.S. troops from Iraq, which the United States invaded in 2003. Meanwhile, the United States has accused Iran of arming and training "criminal" Shiite militias in Iraq and of seeking to develop nuclear weapons, allegations the Iranians deny. It is al-Maliki's third visit to Iran since he became prime minister more than two years ago. The two countries, which are neighbors, both have Shiite Muslim majorities, and al-Maliki's ruling coalition is dominated by Shiite religious parties long backed by Iran. Adnan Pachachi, a leading Sunni Arab member of Iraq's parliament, told CNN he wanted al-Maliki to call on Iran to stop supporting armed factions in Iraq. "I think this has to stop," Pachachi told CNN. "I hope that Mr. Maliki will make it absolutely clear that Iraqis of all parties, of all sectarian origins and ethnic origins, are strongly opposed to Iran's attempt to interfere in Iraq's affairs." Pachachi, a former foreign minister, said al-Maliki's predecessor, Ibrahim al-Jaafari, allowed Iraq's security forces to be dominated by sectarian and ethnic militias, and that U.S. troops should remain until those influences are weeded out. "In the long run, it is in the interest of the United States to have a secure Iraq and armed forces and security forces of Iraq with undivided loyalty and allegiance to the state and not influenced by sectarian affiliations or party loyalties," he said.

Keywords: TEHRAN, Iran, CNN

outputs.L1:
TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki sought on Sunday to ease Iranian concerns regarding a proposed U.S.-Iraq security pact, assuring officials that his government would not permit Iraq to be used as a staging ground for an attack on its neighbor.

During a meeting with Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, al-Maliki stated, "Iraq today does not pose any threat, as it once did under the former regime," according to a statement issued by the prime minister's office. He further remarked, "Today's Iraq is a constitutional state grounded in the rule of law, and it seeks to strengthen its relations with regional countries on the basis of cooperation and mutual respect."

Earlier, Iran's state-run news agency IRNA quoted al-Maliki as saying that "Baghdad would not allow its territory to be used as a base for undermining the security of neighboring countries, including Iran."

These remarks come at a time when the United States and Iraq are negotiating a bilateral agreement concerning the duration of the U.S. military presence in Iraq and its role in the country's security. However, al-Maliki's media adviser, Ali Hadi, clarified that negotiations between Iraq and the United States remain in their "very early stages" and were not part of Sunday's discussions.

"The treaty is purely an Iraqi-American matter. The Iranians have no part in it," Hadi said. "We will not discuss the progress or key elements of any agreements or disagreements with them, as this is strictly an Iraqi issue."

The proposed U.S.-Iraqi pact has sparked street protests across Iraq, where many fear the agreement could pave the way for permanent American military bases, an extended U.S. troop presence, and diminished Iraqi government oversight of foreign forces. Shiite cleric Muqtada al-Sadr—whose militia was recently targeted in a U.S.-backed Iraqi crackdown in Basra and Baghdad—has called for weekly demonstrations against the deal.

Al-Maliki and Ahmadinejad convened Sunday afternoon, with Ahmadinejad urging Iraq's neighboring countries and the United Nations to assist in restoring security and stability to Iraq, according to IRNA. In turn, al-Maliki expressed gratitude to Ahmadinejad for advocating an end to the long-standing U.N. sanctions imposed on Iraq following the 1991 Persian Gulf War.

Iran has consistently called for the withdrawal of U.S. troops from Iraq since the 2003 invasion. Meanwhile, the United States has accused Iran of arming and training "criminal" Shiite militias within Iraq, as well as pursuing nuclear weapons development—allegations Tehran denies.

This marks al-Maliki's third visit to Iran since assuming the role of prime minister more than two years ago. The neighboring nations share a Shiite Muslim majority, and al-Maliki's ruling coalition is largely composed of Shiite religious parties that have long enjoyed Iranian backing.

Adnan Pachachi, a prominent Sunni Arab member of Iraq's parliament, told CNN that he hoped al-Maliki would urge Iran to cease its support for armed factions within Iraq. "I think this has to stop," Pachachi said. "I hope Mr. al-Maliki will make it unequivocally clear that Iraqis of all political parties, sectarian backgrounds, and ethnic origins strongly oppose Iran's interference in Iraq's internal affairs."

Pachachi, a former Iraqi foreign minister, noted that al-Maliki's predecessor, Ibrahim al-Jaafari, had allowed Iraq's security forces to fall under the influence of sectarian and ethnic militias. He argued that U.S. troops should remain in Iraq until such influences are fully eliminated.

"In the long run," Pachachi said, "it is in the interest of the United States to see a secure Iraq—with armed and security forces whose undivided loyalty lies with the state, free from the influence of sectarian affiliations or party allegiances."

TEHRAN, Iran (CNN) -- During a Sunday visit to Iran, Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki sought to ease concerns that a proposed security arrangement between Baghdad and Washington might threaten Iranian interests, assuring officials that his government would never permit Iraqi territory to serve as a staging ground for attacks against Iran. In talks with Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, al-Maliki emphasized that modern Iraq bears little resemblance to the threat it once posed under the previous regime, according to a statement released by his office.

"The Iraq of today operates as a constitutional state governed by rule of law, and aims to build ties with countries in the region grounded in partnership and mutual esteem," al-Maliki stated during the meeting.

Prior to this, Iran's official news agency IRNA cited the Iraqi premier as pledging that Baghdad would never permit its land to be exploited as a launching point for undermining the security of neighboring nations, Iran included.

These comments emerge at a time when Washington and Baghdad are working through negotiations for a bilateral pact determining the duration of American military presence in Iraq and its future security responsibilities there. However, al-Maliki's media adviser, Ali Hadi, clarified that discussions between Iraq and the U.S. remain in "very early stages" and were not addressed during Sunday's session.

"This is strictly a matter between Iraq and America. Iran has no involvement whatsoever," Hadi explained. "We won't be sharing details about how negotiations are progressing or the specific points of agreement or contention with them, since this concerns Iraq alone."

The suggested security framework between the U.S. and Iraq has sparked demonstrations across Iraqi cities, with many citizens worried it could pave the way for permanent American military installations, an extended troop presence, and diminished Iraqi authority over foreign forces. Muqtada al-Sadr, the Shiite cleric whose militia was recently targeted in U.S.-supported operations in Basra and Baghdad, has organized ongoing weekly protests opposing the deal.

During their afternoon meeting, Ahmadinejad urged both Iraq's neighboring states and the United Nations to play a role in bringing stability back to Iraq, per IRNA's report. In response, al-Maliki expressed gratitude to Ahmadinejad for advocating the removal of longstanding U.N. sanctions imposed on Iraq since the 1991 Gulf War.

Tehran has consistently pushed for American forces to leave Iraq following the 2003 invasion. For its part, Washington has charged Iran with supplying weapons and training to what it calls "criminal" Shiite militia groups operating in Iraq, as well as pursuing nuclear weapons capabilities—accusations Tehran rejects.

This marks the third time al-Maliki has traveled to Iran since assuming the premiership over two years ago. The neighboring nations share a Shiite Muslim majority population, and religious Shiite parties with historical Iranian backing form the core of al-Maliki's governing coalition.

Adnan Pachachi, a prominent Sunni Arab lawmaker in Iraq's parliament, expressed to CNN his hope that al-Maliki would press Iran to halt its backing of armed groups within Iraq. "This needs to end," he said. "I want Mr. Maliki to state unambiguously that Iraqis across all political, sectarian, and ethnic lines firmly reject Iranian meddling in Iraqi affairs."

Pachachi, who previously served as foreign minister, noted that under al-Maliki's predecessor Ibrahim al-Jaafari, sectarian and ethnic militias gained significant influence within Iraq's security apparatus. He argued that American troops should stay until such influences are eliminated.

"Ultimately, America benefits from having a stable Iraq with security and military forces that answer solely to the state, free from sectarian or partisan pressures," he added.

# Al-Maliki Assures Iran on Regional Security Concerns Amid U.S. Pact Negotiations

Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki sought to allay Iranian concerns over regional security during a meeting with President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad on Sunday, offering firm assurances that Iraqi territory would not be exploited as a base for hostile actions against neighboring countries. The statement appears designed to reassure Tehran that Baghdad's evolving relationship with Washington poses no threat to Iranian interests or security.

In his remarks, al-Maliki drew a clear distinction between the current Iraqi government and the previous regime under Saddam Hussein, which had a history of military aggression against neighboring states, including Iran itself during the devastating 1980-1988 war. The prime minister emphasized that contemporary Iraq functions as a constitutional democracy operating under the rule of law, positioning the country as a partner for regional cooperation and stability rather than a source of threat or instability. This characterization reflects Iraq's broader efforts to rebrand itself on the international stage as it continues rebuilding its institutions and international relationships.

The timing of these assurances is notable, coming amid sensitive and ongoing negotiations between Iraqi and American officials over a bilateral security agreement that will determine the future scope, duration, and legal framework governing U.S. military presence in Iraq. This pact represents one of the most consequential diplomatic undertakings for Iraq's sovereignty and its relationships with both Western and regional powers.

Addressing questions about Iran's potential role in or reaction to these negotiations, al-Maliki's media adviser was quick to clarify the nature of the discussions, stating that talks between Washington and Baghdad remain in preliminary stages. The adviser stressed that these negotiations constitute a strictly bilateral matter between Iraq and the United States, explicitly excluding any Iranian involvement or influence in the process—a clarification likely intended to preempt criticism that Iraq might be caught between competing American and Iranian interests.

However, the proposed security arrangement has not been without domestic controversy. The pact has ignited significant public unease within Iraq, manifesting in street protests across various cities. Critics and demonstrators have voiced concerns that the agreement could pave the way for a long-term or even permanent American military footprint in the country, undermining Iraq's sovereignty. Additionally, there are fears that the terms of the pact might grant U.S. forces expanded operational latitude while simultaneously reducing the Iraqi government's oversight and control over American military activities on its soil. These concerns reflect broader anxieties among segments of the Iraqi population about the long-term implications of the U.S. military relationship for national independence and self-determination.

# Iraqi PM Seeks to Reassure Iran Over U.S. Security Pact

Baghdad — Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki held talks with Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad this week in an effort to address Tehran's growing unease over a proposed long-term security agreement between Iraq and the United States. The meeting came amid heightened tensions in the region, with Iran expressing concern that the pact could pave the way for American military operations against it, potentially using Iraqi territory as a staging ground.

During the discussions, al-Maliki offered direct assurances to the Iranian leader, stating unequivocally that Iraq would not allow its soil to be used as a launching pad for any military action against Iran or any other neighboring country. The Iraqi prime minister sought to frame the agreement not as a threat to regional stability, but as a necessary step in Iraq's ongoing transition toward full sovereignty.

"Iraq today is a sovereign state governed by the rule of law," al-Maliki said, emphasizing that his government's foreign policy goals center on fostering cooperative and constructive relationships with all countries in the region, including Iran. He stressed that Baghdad's intent is to build partnerships based on mutual respect and non-interference, rather than allow itself to become a tool for outside powers pursuing conflict with its neighbors.

At the same time, a senior adviser to al-Maliki moved to clarify the nature of the ongoing negotiations between Iraq and the United States, underscoring that these talks are a strictly bilateral affair. The adviser stated firmly that Iran has no role in shaping the terms of the agreement and that the negotiations exclude any third-party involvement, signaling Baghdad's intention to keep the process independent of outside pressure — from Tehran or elsewhere.

The proposed security pact, which would govern the presence and operations of U.S. forces in Iraq beyond the expiration of the current United Nations mandate, has become a source of significant domestic controversy. Critics within Iraq, including various political factions and segments of the public, have voiced strong objections to the deal, fearing it could formalize a long-term or even permanent American military presence in the country. These concerns have fueled protests across Iraq, with demonstrators demanding greater transparency in the negotiations and guarantees that any agreement will not compromise Iraqi sovereignty or drag the country into future conflicts.

As al-Maliki's government navigates these competing pressures — balancing its security partnership with Washington against the diplomatic sensitivities of its relationship with Tehran, as well as public opinion at home — the outcome of the negotiations remains closely watched both regionally and internationally.

# Tehran: Iran's Capital in the Global Spotlight

Tehran, the sprawling capital of Iran, stands as one of the most strategically significant cities in the Middle East. Home to over 8 million residents in the city proper and more than 15 million in its greater metropolitan area, Tehran serves as the political, economic, and cultural heart of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

Nestled at the foot of the Alborz mountain range, Tehran has grown from a relatively modest settlement into a sprawling metropolis over the past century. The city hosts Iran's key governmental institutions, including the presidential offices, parliament (Majlis), and numerous ministries that shape the nation's domestic and foreign policy.

International media outlets, including CNN, regularly report on developments emanating from Tehran, given Iran's significant role in regional and global affairs. CNN's coverage often focuses on several recurring themes: Iran's nuclear program and negotiations with world powers, the country's complex relationship with the United States and its allies, regional tensions involving Iran's influence in neighboring countries, and domestic issues such as economic sanctions, protests, and human rights concerns.

CNN, as one of the world's leading 24-hour news networks, plays a substantial role in shaping how international audiences perceive events unfolding in Tehran. The network's correspondents and analysts provide context on Iranian politics, often featuring interviews with officials, experts, and citizens to offer multiple perspectives on complex situations.

Coverage of Tehran by international networks like CNN has historically intensified during periods of heightened tension—whether related to nuclear negotiations, military incidents in the region, internal political protests, or diplomatic breakthroughs. These reports help shape global public opinion and inform policy discussions in Washington, European capitals, and beyond.

However, reporting on Iran presents unique challenges for international journalists. Access restrictions, government oversight of foreign media, and the complexity of Iranian society mean that coverage sometimes struggles to capture the full nuance of daily life in Tehran, where millions of ordinary citizens navigate economic pressures, cultural richness, and political constraints simultaneously.

As geopolitical dynamics in the Middle East continue to evolve, Tehran will likely remain a focal point for international news coverage, with outlets like CNN continuing to serve as a primary lens through which global audiences understand developments in this historically significant and strategically important city.

counterfactuals.output:
# Maliki Seeks Iranian Backing Amid Security Pact Negotiations

**BAGHDAD/TEHRAN** — Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki traveled to Tehran this week for high-level talks with Iranian officials, a visit that underscored the delicate balancing act Baghdad continues to perform between its two most influential foreign partners, the United States and Iran.

The trip came as negotiators from Washington and Baghdad work to finalize a long-term security agreement that would govern the presence of American forces in Iraq beyond the expiration of the current United Nations mandate at the end of the year.

During meetings with Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad and Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, al-Maliki sought to reassure his hosts that any deal with Washington would not compromise Iraqi sovereignty or serve as a launching pad for military action against Iran.

"Iraq will not allow its territory to be used as a base to threaten the security of neighboring countries," al-Maliki said in remarks carried by Iraqi state media, a statement clearly aimed at easing Iranian anxieties over the pending pact.

Iranian officials have repeatedly criticized draft versions of the agreement, characterizing early proposals as an infringement on Iraqi sovereignty that could grant the U.S. sweeping legal immunities and open-ended basing rights. Ahmadinejad, in public comments alongside al-Maliki, reiterated Tehran's position that foreign forces should ultimately withdraw from Iraq.

Al-Maliki, for his part, struck a note of independence, telling reporters that Baghdad would not sign any agreement that failed to protect Iraqi interests, regardless of pressure from either side.

"We are looking for a balanced agreement that respects Iraq's sovereignty," he said. "We will not accept a deal that does not serve the interests of the Iraqi people."

The visit highlights the complex position al-Maliki occupies as he navigates relationships with two governments that view each other with deep suspicion. Washington has repeatedly accused Tehran of arming and funding Shiite militias inside Iraq, allegations Iranian officials deny. At the same time, the U.S. has relied on al-Maliki's government as a partner in stabilizing the country following years of sectarian violence.

Analysts say the Tehran visit was as much about optics as substance, allowing al-Maliki to demonstrate to his domestic constituency — and to Iraq's Shiite-majority population, which shares religious and cultural ties with Iran — that he is not simply acquiescing to American demands.

Negotiations over the security agreement, formally known as the Status of Forces Agreement, are expected to continue in the coming weeks. Sticking points reportedly include the legal jurisdiction over U.S. troops accused of crimes on Iraqi soil, the duration of the American military presence, and limits on U.S. combat operations.

U.S. officials have declined to comment directly on al-Maliki's Tehran trip but have said they remain confident that an agreement can be reached that satisfies both Iraqi sovereignty concerns and American security requirements.

Iraqi officials have said they hope to conclude negotiations before the U.N. mandate authorizing foreign forces expires, though they have not ruled out seeking a short-term extension if a final deal is not reached in time.

*This is a developing story.*

# Iraqi PM Maliki's Tehran Visit Draws Sunni Criticism Amid Regional Diplomatic Push

**Baghdad/Tehran** — Iraqi Prime Minister Nuri al-Maliki's visit to Tehran has drawn sharp criticism from Sunni political figures, who argue the trip reinforces perceptions of excessive Iranian influence over Baghdad's government and deepens sectarian divisions within Iraq.

## The Visit

Maliki traveled to the Iranian capital as part of ongoing efforts to strengthen bilateral ties between the two neighboring, Shia-majority-led states. During his discussions with senior Iranian officials, talks reportedly touched on security cooperation, economic ties, trade relations, and coordination on regional stability issues affecting both countries.

Iranian officials have consistently framed the Iraq relationship as a priority, given shared borders, religious ties, and mutual security concerns tied to instability following the 2003 U.S.-led invasion.

## Sunni Political Reaction

The visit has reignited longstanding concerns among Iraq's Sunni Arab political class, who have repeatedly accused Maliki's government of being too closely aligned with Tehran at the expense of Iraq's Sunni population and broader Arab identity.

**Adnan Pachachi**, the veteran Iraqi statesman and former foreign minister who has long been viewed as a moderate voice within Sunni politics, voiced concern over the trajectory of Iraqi-Iranian relations. Pachachi has previously warned that overly close ties with Tehran risk undermining Iraq's sovereignty and its standing among Arab neighbors, many of whom view Iranian influence in Iraq with suspicion.

Sunni critics more broadly have pointed to the frequency and tone of high-level exchanges between Baghdad and Tehran as evidence that Maliki's government prioritizes sectarian and religious affinity with Iran over national unity and inclusive governance.

## Broader Context

These criticisms reflect deeper structural tensions in post-2003 Iraq, where the collapse of the Sunni-dominated Baathist state and the empowerment of Iraq's Shia majority through elections opened the door to closer Baghdad-Tehran relations. Sunni politicians have frequently argued that:

- Iranian influence undermines Iraq's Arab character and regional alliances
- Maliki's government has marginalized Sunni voices in security and political institutions
- Closer ties with Iran complicate Iraq's relationships with Gulf Arab states and Washington

## Outlook

The visit is likely to intensify debate within Iraq's fractured political landscape over the country's foreign policy orientation, particularly as Sunni, Kurdish, and secular Shia factions continue to negotiate their place within a political system reshaped by the post-invasion order. Analysts suggest that unresolved tensions over Iranian influence will remain a recurring flashpoint in Iraqi politics as long as sectarian power-sharing arrangements remain fragile.

---

*Note: This report reflects a composite account based on the type of coverage and political dynamics common to this period; specific dates, quotes, and details should be verified against primary news sources for accuracy in any final publication.*

**Tehran Voices Alarm Over Proposed U.S.-Iraq Security Pact**

*Tehran* — Iranian officials have escalated criticism of a proposed long-term security agreement between the United States and Iraq, warning that the pact could undermine regional stability and infringe on Iraqi sovereignty.

The agreement under discussion would govern the legal status of U.S. forces in Iraq and potentially outline a longer-term American military presence following the expiration of the United Nations mandate authorizing coalition operations. Details of the negotiations have not been fully disclosed publicly, but reports suggest the framework could address troop numbers, military bases, legal jurisdiction over U.S. personnel, and the scope of American operations within Iraqi territory.

Senior Iranian figures, including officials within the government and members of parliament, have characterized the deal as a potential vehicle for indefinite U.S. military entrenchment in Iraq. Tehran has repeatedly framed any long-term American troop presence in the region as a threat to its own security interests, given the countries' shared border and historical ties.

Iranian state media and officials have called on the Iraqi government to ensure that any agreement respects full Iraqi sovereignty and does not grant U.S. forces expansive legal immunities or unrestricted operational freedom. Some Iranian commentators have also suggested that the negotiations could be used to position U.S. forces or intelligence operations in ways that could be directed against neighboring countries, a concern that has not been substantiated by Washington or Baghdad.

Iraqi officials have pushed back on characterizations that the deal would cede excessive sovereignty, stating that any final agreement would need parliamentary approval and would reflect Iraqi national interests. Iraqi political factions, including some with close ties to Tehran, have also weighed in, with several blocs expressing reservations about granting U.S. troops broad legal protections or open-ended basing rights.

The controversy underscores the complex three-way dynamic between Washington, Baghdad, and Tehran, as Iraq navigates its relationships with both the United States, which maintains a significant military footprint from the post-2003 era, and Iran, a powerful neighbor with deep religious, economic, and political influence in Iraq.

Analysts note that the outcome of the negotiations will likely have lasting implications for the balance of power in the region, as both Washington and Tehran seek to safeguard their respective strategic interests in a country still rebuilding from years of conflict.

*This report reflects publicly available information current as of recent developments; specific terms of the agreement remain subject to ongoing negotiation and have not been finalized.*

# Maliki Assures Iran Regarding U.S.-Iraq Military Pact Amid Protests

**BAGHDAD, Iraq** — Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki has moved to reassure Iranian officials that a proposed security agreement with the United States will not be used as a platform for any military action against Iran, as demonstrators took to the streets of Baghdad to protest the deal.

The proposed pact, which would govern the status of American troops in Iraq beyond the current United Nations mandate, has become a flashpoint for critics who fear it could compromise Iraqi sovereignty and drag the country into a broader regional conflict with its eastern neighbor.

Maliki's government has been engaged in delicate negotiations with Washington over the terms of the agreement, even as it seeks to maintain Baghdad's increasingly important relationship with Tehran. Iranian officials have repeatedly voiced concern that the deal could allow U.S. forces to use Iraqi territory as a staging ground for operations against Iran.

"We have made clear to our Iranian brothers that Iraq will not become a launching pad for any aggression against Iran or any other neighboring state," a senior Iraqi official close to the negotiations said, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions.

The assurances come at a politically delicate moment for Maliki, whose Shiite-led government relies on support from factions with close ties to Tehran, even as it depends on the continued presence of American forces for security assistance.

## Protests Mount in Baghdad

Thousands of demonstrators, many of them followers of the anti-American cleric Muqtada al-Sadr, gathered in Baghdad to denounce the proposed agreement, chanting slogans against what they characterized as an open-ended U.S. military presence in Iraq. Protesters carried banners denouncing the pact as an infringement on national sovereignty and called on the government to reject any deal that did not include a firm timetable for the withdrawal of foreign troops.

Sadrist lawmakers in the Iraqi parliament have been among the most vocal opponents of the agreement, warning that it could grant the United States sweeping powers within Iraq for years to come, including control over Iraqi airspace and immunity from prosecution for American contractors and soldiers.

"This agreement, as it is being negotiated, is a humiliation to the Iraqi people," said one Sadrist member of parliament during a rally outside the Green Zone. "We will not accept any pact that ties the fate of Iraq to American interests indefinitely."

## Balancing Two Allies

Analysts say Maliki finds himself in an increasingly difficult position, attempting to balance Iraq's dependence on U.S. military support with its need to maintain stable relations with Iran, a country with deep religious, economic and political ties to Iraq's Shiite majority.

Iranian President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's government has publicly criticized draft versions of the agreement, with Iranian officials warning that any long-term U.S. military presence in Iraq poses a direct threat to regional stability.

Iraqi officials have sought to walk a careful line, insisting that the agreement is strictly bilateral and does not envision any role for Iraqi territory in potential hostilities involving third countries.

"Iraq's territory, airspace and waters will not be used to threaten the security of neighboring countries," Iraqi government spokesman Ali al-Dabbagh said in a statement, reiterating language that negotiators have reportedly sought to include in the final text of the agreement.

Despite such assurances, skepticism remains high among Iraqi lawmakers, with some questioning whether the government can guarantee such provisions will be honored in practice once U.S. forces' legal status is formalized under the new framework.

## Path Forward Uncertain

The Iraqi government has faced mounting pressure from parliament to disclose the full text of the draft agreement, with many lawmakers complaining they have been kept in the dark about key details of the negotiations. Under Iraq's constitution, the pact will require parliamentary approval before it can take effect.

With the current U.N. mandate authorizing the U.S. military presence in Iraq set to expire at the end of the year, both governments face a narrowing window to finalize an agreement — one that Maliki must now navigate while managing the competing expectations of Washington, Tehran and an increasingly restive Iraqi public.

*This report includes information gathered from Iraqi government statements and parliamentary sources in Baghdad.*
